extracted.intended_audience: students, instructors, writers, and editors seeking instruction in plain English style
extracted.subtask_description: A concise style guide describing elementary rules of usage, principles of composition, and matters of form for clear, vigorous English prose. Intended to be used by writers and teachers to evaluate and produce correct, effective writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this rule whatever the final consonant (Charles's friend; Burns's poems; the witch's malice). Exceptions: possessives of certain ancient proper names in -es and -is, the possessive Jesus', and set phrases like for conscience' sake. Common alternatives (the heel of Achilles, the laws of Moses) are acceptable. Pronominal possessives (hers, its, theirs, yours, oneself) have no apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a comma after each term in a series of three or more
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: red, white, and blue; He opened the letter, read it, and made a note of its contents. This is the Government Printing Office and Oxford University Press usage. Exception: in names of business firms the last comma is omitted (Brown, Shipley & Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a word or phrase is parenthetic; if interruption is slight, commas may be omitted, but never insert one comma and omit the other. Place the first comma before a conjunction if the parenthetic expression follows it. Always consider as parenthetic (and set off with commas): the year in a date and the day of the month when following the weekday; abbreviations such as etc. and jr.; non-restrictive relative clauses (those that do not identify the antecedent). Similar principle applies to setting off phrases or dependent clauses that precede or follow the main clause. Anti-patterns: setting off independent clauses by commas (see Rule 5) and omitting paired commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The early records of the city have disappeared, and the story of its first years can no longer be reconstructed. Use a comma before and, but, or nor introducing an independent clause. Two-part sentences where the second member begins with as (because), for, or, nor, while (in sense 'and at the same time') likewise require a comma. If the second member is introduced by an adverb (accordingly, therefore, etc.) and not a conjunction, use a semicolon (see Rule 5). Connectives 'so' and 'yet' may function as adverbs or conjunctions; punctuation depends on function. If a dependent clause or introductory phrase precedes the second independent clause, no comma is needed after the conjunction. When the subject is the same and expressed once, use a comma with 'but'; omit with 'and' if relation is close or immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not join independent clauses by a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more clauses are grammatically complete and not joined by a conjunction, do not join them with a comma; use a semicolon or a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolon to connect independent clauses (Stevenson's romances are entertaining; they are full of exciting adventures). Period is also permissible (as two sentences). If a conjunction is used, use a comma (Rule 4). If the second clause begins with an adverb such as accordingly, therefore, then, use a semicolon. Exceptions: very short, similarly formed clauses may be linked by a comma (Man proposes, God disposes). Colloquial constructions (I hardly knew him, he was so changed,) use a comma but are inappropriate in formal writing except in dialogue or informal letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not break sentences in two
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not break sentences in two—that is, do not use periods where commas are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace erroneous periods with commas when the following phrase belongs to the same sentence. Sentence fragments used for emphasis are permissible (Again and again he called out. No reply.) but must be used sparingly and only when the emphasis is warranted; beware of producing what looks like a punctuation or syntactic blunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: A participial phrase at the beginning must refer to the grammatical subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dangling modifiers: Walking slowly down the road, he saw a woman... (walking refers to he, not the woman). If you intend the participle to modify a different noun, recast the sentence (He saw a woman..., walking slowly down the road). The same rule applies to participial phrases preceded by conjunctions or prepositions, nouns in apposition, adjectives, and adjective phrases when they begin the sentence. Examples and corrected rewrites show ludicrous or misleading results when this rule is violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is slight, a single paragraph may suffice; ordinarily subdivide by topic, each topic becoming a paragraph. Paragraphs signal to the reader a new step in development. Extent of subdivision depends on composition length; examples provided for book notices, poem reports, novels, and historical events show how to subdivide topics. Avoid single-sentence paragraphs except for transitions or in dialogue (each speech is a paragraph). After drafting, examine paragraphs to see whether subdivision would improve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, begin each paragraph with a topic sentence and end it in conformity with the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended paragraph structure: (a) topic sentence at or near beginning, (b) succeeding sentences explain/develop the topic sentence, (c) final sentence emphasizes the topic sentence or states a consequence. Avoid ending with digressions or unimportant details. Transitional sentences may precede the topic sentence when needed; if multiple transitions required, consider making them a separate paragraph. Ways to develop the topic sentence: restatement, definition, denial of contrary, illustrations, proofs, implications. Examples from Stevenson and Lecky are annotated to show paragraph function. In narration and description, paragraphs may begin with a concise statement holding details together; brief narrative paragraphs may omit a formal topic sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the active voice—it's usually more direct and vigorous than the passive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions (I shall always remember... vs. My first visit... will always be remembered by me). Passive is acceptable when needed to make a particular word the subject or for variety. Avoid making one passive depend on another; avoid passives that place an action noun as the subject with a weak verb (A survey of this region was made in 1900 → This region was surveyed in 1900). Habitual use of active voice strengthens writing; many tame sentences can be improved by substituting an active verb for perfunctory 'there is' constructions. Examples show transformations to more forceful phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put statements in positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: Put statements in positive form—make definite assertions and avoid evasive or non-committal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'not' as means of evasion. Prefer direct positive words and concise expressions (He usually came late vs. He was not very often on time). Rewrite negatives into positives when possible (not honest → dishonest; did not remember → forgot). Use negative only for denial or antithesis. Provide examples showing stronger positive alternatives and note that many negative words other than 'not' can be strong (The sun never sets upon the British flag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use definite, specific, concrete language; prefer the specific to the general and the concrete to the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific detail arouses and holds the reader's attention; literary examples (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Browning) illustrate effectiveness of concreteness. When discussing general principles in exposition/argument, give particular instances of application. Quoted commentary (Herbert Spencer) explains why specific expressions are superior: readers think in particulars, so specific images are more immediate and vivid. Examples show concrete rewrites of vague sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit needless words—be concise; every word should tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vigorous writing is concise; don't make all sentences short, but eliminate unnecessary words and phrases (the question as to whether → whether; there is no doubt but that → no doubt). The phrase 'the fact that' should be revised out wherever possible (owing to the fact that → since). 'Who is', 'which was', etc., are often superfluous. Positive statements and active voice aid concision. Avoid presenting a complex idea in a series of short sentences when one combined sentence would be clearer and shorter; examples compare verbose and concise versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a succession of loose sentences—do not construct paragraphs of many similar loose sentences formed of two coordinate clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loose sentences of the type 'main clause, and + second clause' are acceptable singly but a series becomes monotonous and tedious. Overuse of connectives (and, but, so, who, which, when, where, while in non-restrictive senses) weakens writing. Example paragraph demonstrates triteness and weakness caused by repetitively structured loose sentences; writer should vary sentence forms and avoid an entire paragraph of this pattern.
